prompt.context: A major auto service chain, Wheeler Dealer, has enjoyed healthy returns on its 30-store operation for the past 10 years. However, management feels that the chain needs to expand, as the current geographical areas in which they are based have become saturated. For the past couple of years, they have aggressively pursued a growth strategy, opening an additional 15 stores. However, it seems that this approach has had negative returns. For the first time in over a decade, the chain's profits dropped into the negative zone.
prompt.question: You were hired to figure out why Wheeler Dealer's profits turned negative after expanding from 30 to 45 stores.

clarifying_info.q: What type of services does Wheeler Dealer provide?
clarifying_info.a: There are two main businesses under each roof: off-the-shelf car parts (retail) and garage mechanical services.

clarifying_info.q: Are both services offered at the new stores as well?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, both services are provided at the new stores.

clarifying_info.q: Have competitors entered the market and stolen market share?
clarifying_info.a: A few competitors have entered the market, but not too many. The expansion was planned to explore new markets and prevent the competition from growing.

clarifying_info.q: Have prices changed to help offset the costs of growth?
clarifying_info.a: No, prices have stayed the same.

clarifying_info.q: Do the two business lines carry the same profit margin?
clarifying_info.a: No. Garage mechanical services have twice the profit margin of off-the-shelf products. Mechanics are highly trained and the business charges a premium.

clarifying_info.q: Are the customers the same for both business lines?
clarifying_info.a: No. Garage service customers tend to come from a mid-to-high income bracket. Off-the-shelf auto parts customers tend to be lower-income; they fix their own cars.

clarifying_info.q: Where has Wheeler Dealer traditionally been located?
clarifying_info.a: Mostly in, or very close to, the suburbs.

clarifying_info.q: Has the geographical location changed with the expansion?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. They saw certain urban areas as inexpensive and located more stores in inner cities where there are a lot of used car sales.

framework: Understand the nature of the business: two distinct revenue streams (off-the-shelf parts vs. garage mechanical services) under one roof
Analyze customer segmentation: are both segments being served equally across old and new stores?
Examine profit structure of each offering: compare margins between the two business lines
Investigate the new store locations: did the geographical shift change the customer mix?
Apply Profitability Framework: assess how revenue composition has changed given the new environment

questions.prompt: What are the two business lines at Wheeler Dealer and how do their profit margins compare?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies that Wheeler Dealer operates two distinct lines: (1) off-the-shelf car parts retail and (2) garage mechanical services. The garage service carries twice the profit margin of the parts retail business because mechanics are highly trained and the business charges a premium. This asymmetry is the key to unlocking the profitability problem.

questions.prompt: How does the customer base differ between the two business lines, and what does that imply about location strategy?
questions.guidance: Garage service customers are mid-to-high income suburban customers. Off-the-shelf parts customers are lower-income, often inner-city residents who fix their own cars. The original 30 stores were located in or near suburbs, attracting the higher-margin garage customers. The 15 new stores moved into inexpensive urban/inner-city areas, shifting the customer mix toward the lower-margin parts segment.

questions.prompt: Synthesize the root cause: why did profits turn negative after expansion?
questions.guidance: The expansion into inner-city areas attracted customers who predominantly use the lower-margin off-the-shelf parts business rather than the high-margin garage service. With garage service margin at 2x the parts margin, a meaningful shift in revenue mix toward parts—without any price increase—is insufficient to cover operating costs and deliver a positive return. Key finding: the garage service is the major revenue generator; the parts margin alone cannot sustain the cost structure.

recommendation: Scale back from urban area stores that are unable to attract suburban customers for the high-margin garage service
Focus geographic expansion on suburban and near-suburban areas where mid-to-high income customers will use the service aspect of the business
Where possible, drop the garage service in under-performing urban locations to reduce costs and focus solely on the retail parts end
risks: Retreat from inner cities may cede those markets permanently to competitors
Closing or restructuring stores involves significant exit costs and potential write-downs
Concentrating on suburban markets increases geographic concentration risk if those markets become saturated or face new entrants
next_steps: Conduct a store-level profitability analysis to identify which of the 15 new stores have viable suburban customer bases
Develop criteria (income demographics, suburban proximity, used-car-ownership rates) for evaluating future expansion locations
Model the revenue and margin impact of removing garage services from the weakest urban stores before committing to full closures
